figures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
also_known_as: one of the three Cappadocian Fathers
figures.places: Cappadocia and Pontus (Caesarea, the family estate at Annisa, Nyssa); Constantinople for the council of 381; travelled to Arabia and Jerusalem c. 381-382
figures.role: Younger brother of Basil the Great and of Macrina; teacher of rhetoric before ordination; bishop of Nyssa from 372; deposed and exiled 376-378 under the pro-Arian emperor Valens; a leading voice at the Council of Constantinople (381); philosopher-theologian and mystical writer
figures.status_note: Saint in the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran traditions (feast 9 or 10 January in the East, 9 March in the West). The Second Council of Nicaea (787) called him 'father of fathers'. Caution for readers: he openly hoped that all evil, and even the devil, would finally be healed (apokatastasis). He was never condemned by name, but Origenist teaching on this was condemned in 553, and an 8th-century patriarch (Germanus of Constantinople) claimed his books had been tampered with. He was probably married (he says a 'gulf' divides him from virginity); the name of a wife, Theosebia, is disputed.
figures.hook: He forged letters from his uncle to patch up a family feud, got caught more than once, and his brother Basil wrote to tell him he was too simple to be trusted; he became the boldest mind of his family, the one who hoped even the devil would be healed.

stories.story: Trying to reconcile Basil with their uncle, a bishop, Gregory forged a letter in the uncle's name and brought it to Basil, who showed it round delightedly until the uncle denied writing it. Then came a second, and a third. Basil wrote back: 'How can I lay hold of you satisfactorily, with all your simplicity? Tell me; who ever falls a third time into the same nets?'
stories.source: Basil the Great, Letter 58 (To Gregory my brother), NPNF2 vol. 8

stories.story: After about eight years of exile and church trouble he went to see his sister Macrina and found her dying. When he poured out his complaints about his exile under Valens and his conflicts, she told him to stop being ungrateful: churches summoned him everywhere, and it was their parents' prayers, not his own equipment, that lifted him. The next day she died, and he wrote her Life.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (trans. W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1916)

stories.story: Grieving Basil's death, he went to Macrina to weep with her. She let him cry a while, then argued with him. He blurted out that Scripture's promise of the soul's survival felt to him like a bare command without reasons; she made him argue the unbeliever's side so they could reason it out. The result is his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection.
stories.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening, NPNF2 vol. 5

stories.story: Returning from exile in 378, he found the road lined with villagers crying for joy; at his church door the crowd pressed so close he nearly fainted, and the virgins' choir marched in with torches like 'a stream of fire'. He rejoiced and wept with his people, then dashed off a letter to a friend before he let himself drink.
stories.source: Letter 3, To Ablabius (NPNF numbering), NPNF2 vol. 5

stories.story: He rode fifteen miles over a road 'like a precipice' to make peace with Bishop Helladius, was left sitting in the sun until noon while people stared at him, was given no seat, no greeting and no meal, and was sent back in a rainstorm. His letter about it swings between Christ-like humility and wounded pride in his own birth and learning.
stories.source: Letter 18, To Flavian (NPNF numbering; Ep. 1 in Pasquali's edition), NPNF2 vol. 5

stories.story: He satirised Constantinople in the 380s, where everyone from money-changers and bread-sellers to runaway slaves argued about the 'Begotten and the Unbegotten' instead of answering a simple question. Schaff reports this from Gregory's sermon On the Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit.
stories.source: Gregory of Nyssa, De deitate Filii et Spiritus Sancti (PG 46.557), as reported in Schaff, History of the Christian Church vol. 3 (1884) sec. 118 with note naming Gregory of Nyssa as the source

stories.story: Not checked against the Greek in this pass: in his second sermon on the Forty Martyrs he tells how, as a young man, he sulked through a family festival for the martyrs, fell asleep, and dreamed the martyrs came at him with rods for his indifference; he woke weeping. Verify in In Quadraginta Martyres (PG 46) before use.
stories.source: In XL Martyres II (secondary report; no public-domain English found)

temperament.evidence: Basil scolds 'your simplicity, which I see plainly to be neither what generally becomes a Christian man, nor is appropriate to the present emergency', and elsewhere calls him 'quite inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs' but also 'a man like my brother, to whom anything like mean servility is unknown'.
temperament.source: Basil, Letter 58 (first quotation, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202058.htm) and Letter 215 (the other two), NPNF2 vol. 8

temperament.trait: Tender, quick to weep, needed his sister to steady him
temperament.evidence: 'My soul was right sorrow-stricken by this grievous blow, and I sought for one who could feel it equally, to mingle my tears with.' Macrina 'gave in to me for a little while, like a skilful driver, in the ungovernable violence of my grief'.
temperament.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection, opening

temperament.trait: Proud of his birth and learning, stung by slights, honest about the fight inside him
temperament.evidence: Snubbed by Helladius he writes that in 'education for instance, or in birth ... or in theology' the two of them 'will be found either equal, or at all events not inferior, in me', while describing 'two contending feelings ... the one, of anger at the insult caused by pride, the other prompting to appease the rising storm'.
Writing to a young classics enthusiast he opens with Homer instead of Scripture and teases himself: 'garrulity is just as characteristic of old age as to be blear-eyed, or for the limbs to fail.'
temperament.source: Letter 8, To a Student of the Classics

temperament.trait: A questioner who says his doubts out loud
temperament.evidence: 'I answered rather audaciously, and without due consideration of what I said, for my passionate grief had not yet given me back my judgment.'
temperament.source: On the Soul and the Resurrection

genuine_lines.quote: Change of place does not effect any drawing nearer unto God, but wherever you may be, God will come to you, if the chambers of your soul be found of such a sort that He can dwell in you and walk in you.
genuine_lines.translation: William Moore and H. A. Wilson, NPNF2 vol. 5 (1893), rev. New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: counsel the brethren to be absent from the body to go to our Lord, rather than to be absent from Cappadocia to go to Palestine

He accomplished all the results before mentioned, freeing both man from evil, and healing even the introducer of evil himself. For the chastisement, however painful, of moral disease is a healing of its weakness.
They therefore do not understand that all virtue is found in moderation, and that any declension to either side of it becomes a vice.
You condemn to slavery a human being, whose nature is free and self-ruling, and you make laws against God, overturning His law for our nature.
genuine_lines.work: Homilies on Ecclesiastes, Homily 4 (on Eccl 2:7, 'I got me slaves and slave-girls')
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Greek: Δουλείᾳ καταδικάζεις τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οὗ ἐλευθέρα ἡ φύσις καὶ αὐτεξούσιος, καὶ ἀντινομοθετεῖς τῷ Θεῷ, ἀνατρέπων αὐτοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει νόμον.

genuine_lines.quote: For what price, tell me? What did you find among the things that exist worth as much as this nature? ... For how many obols did you weigh out the image of God?
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Greek: Ποίας, εἰπέ μοι, τιμῆς; Τί εὗρες ἐν τοῖς οὖσι τῆς φύσεως ταύτης ἀντάξιον; ... Πόσοις ὀβολοῖς τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀντεστάθμησας;

misattributed.line: Concepts create idols; only wonder comprehends anything.
misattributed.truth: A modern condensation, not a sentence Gregory wrote. The thought is real: in Life of Moses II.162-165 he says every concept the mind forms of God becomes an idol (eidolon) of God rather than God. Quote the passage, not the slogan.

misattributed.line: The story that his wife was named Theosebia and that Gregory of Nazianzus wrote her epitaph as his wife.
misattributed.truth: Disputed. Nazianzen's letter of condolence (Ep. 197) mourns a Theosebia connected to Gregory, but whether she was wife or sister is argued. Gregory's own On Virginity 3 is the firm evidence that he had married.

opinions.position: In the end evil will be wholly removed, all will be restored, and even the devil, the 'introducer of evil', will be healed. Punishment is a painful cure, not an endless sentence.
opinions.side_note: Yes side: universal restoration. Rare among the Fathers (Origen, Gregory, Evagrius, Isaac in his second part); most held eternal punishment.
opinions.today: Split among Christians: most traditional Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical teaching rejects it; a growing minority (Hart, Parry, many mainline Protestants) hope for it. Among non-Christians it is the more attractive view. A good discriminator.
opinions.quote: He accomplished all the results before mentioned, freeing both man from evil, and healing even the introducer of evil himself.

opinions.topic: new: punishment after death heals rather than only repays
opinions.position: The fire after death is a refining fire: it burns away the evil stuck to a soul, and it hurts exactly as much as the soul clings to evil, until only the 'gold' is left.
opinions.side_note: Spoken by Macrina in Gregory's dialogue, which he wrote and endorses; the same teaching is in his own voice in the Great Catechism 26 and 35.
opinions.today: Catholics accept a purifying purgatory for the saved but not for all; Orthodox reject a formal purgatory; many Protestants reject both. People outside the churches tend to prefer punishment that heals.
opinions.quote: so, while evil is being consumed in the purgatorial fire, the soul that is welded to this evil must inevitably be in the fire too, until the spurious material alloy is consumed and annihilated by this fire.
opinions.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection

opinions.position: Grief at a death is natural and he felt it violently, but in the end he agreed with his sister that it must be governed by hope in the resurrection and reasoned through, not indulged.
opinions.side_note: Middle side: grieve, but not as those without hope. He voices the case for grief strongly before yielding.
opinions.today: Most people today say grief should be expressed freely and not argued with; many Christians still say 'grieve with hope'. Moderately discriminating.
opinions.quote: She quoted the Apostle's words about the duty of not being grieved for them that sleep; because only men without hope have such feelings.
opinions.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection

opinions.position: Anger, desire and the other passions are not evil in themselves; they are raw material. Used under reason they become tools of virtue; left in charge they become vices.
opinions.side_note: Moderate side: passions are usable, not to be torn out. Contrast the Stoic-leaning desert ideal of apatheia (Evagrius) and his own Moses example, who was 'superior both to anger and to desire'. Words are Macrina's in his dialogue.
opinions.today: Most people today agree emotions are neutral and useful, so this is fairly one-sided now; it divides only from strict ascetic views.
opinions.quote: according to the use which our free will puts them to, these emotions of the soul become the instruments of virtue or of vice. They are like the iron which is being fashioned according to the volition of the artificer, and receives whatever shape the idea which is in his mind prescribes, and becomes a sword or some agricultural implement.
opinions.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection

opinions.position: When insulted he felt anger rise and fought it down to speak peaceably, but he did not pretend the anger away; he admitted both feelings.
opinions.side_note: Mixed: restraint in the moment, honesty about the feeling.
opinions.today: Most people accept 'feel it, don't act on it'. One-sided today unless paired with the question of whether anger itself is sinful.
opinions.quote: This was the very array, in opposition, of two contending feelings that I saw within myself: the one, of anger at the insult caused by pride, the other prompting to appease the rising storm.

opinions.position: A proud colleague who insults an equal should not be left alone for the sake of peace; his pride needs to be brought down to size, though he leaves the method to God.
opinions.side_note: Correct side: confront the offender (while he first tried reconciliation in person).
opinions.today: People split between 'let it go' and 'call it out'; a live question.
opinions.quote: therefore I deem it right to see that this malady of puffed-up pride is not left without a cure; and it will be its cure to put it down to its proper level, and reduce its inflated dimensions, by letting off a little of the conceit with which he is bursting.

opinions.position: Travelling to the holy places brings you no nearer to God; Jerusalem is full of crime, and Cappadocia has more altars. Stay home and make your soul a place God can live in.
opinions.side_note: Against pilgrimage (at least as a duty, especially for monks and women). Nuance: in Letter 17 he describes 'intense joy' at seeing the Sacred Places, so he valued them, but denied they were needed. Protestant polemic long used this letter; its authenticity has been questioned by some Catholic writers but is generally accepted.
opinions.today: Split: many Catholics and Orthodox value pilgrimage; many Protestants and secular people agree with Gregory. Good discriminator; pairs with Jerome's later change of mind.
opinions.quote: Change of place does not effect any drawing nearer unto God, but wherever you may be, God will come to you, if the chambers of your soul be found of such a sort that He can dwell in you and walk in you.

opinions.position: Virginity is the better way, and marriage brings endless fear and grief (for spouse and children); he, a married man, regretted that the better way was closed to him. Yet marriage used soberly is blessed by God and must not be despised.
opinions.side_note: Virginity higher, marriage good. Condemns those who call marriage abominable.
opinions.today: Most people today, Christians included, reject 'celibacy is the higher way'; Catholics and Orthodox keep a version of it. Discriminating.
opinions.quote: Happy they who have still the power of choosing the better way, and have not debarred themselves from it by engagements of the secular life, as we have, whom a gulf now divides from glorious virginity

opinions.position: Discipline must keep the middle way: too little is indulgence, too much slides into the teaching of those who hate marriage and creation. Virtue is moderation.
opinions.side_note: Moderate asceticism.
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees with 'moderation' in the abstract, so the item needs concrete framing to discriminate.
opinions.quote: They therefore do not understand that all virtue is found in moderation, and that any declension to either side of it becomes a vice.

opinions.position: No one may own a human being. A person made in God's image is priceless; buying one sets a price on the image of God and legislates against God. Unique in antiquity for condemning the institution itself, not just cruelty within it.
opinions.side_note: Other Fathers (Augustine, Chrysostom, Basil) urged kindness to slaves but did not condemn owning them. Macrina persuaded their mother to live with her slave women 'as if they were sisters'.
opinions.today: Everyone today agrees slavery is wrong, so as a statement it tells the quiz nothing; its value is in the reveal ('the only Father who said this outright').
opinions.quote: You condemn to slavery a human being, whose nature is free and self-ruling, and you make laws against God, overturning His law for our nature.
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Greek text (Migne) on earlychurchtexts.com; the English on that page is the webmaster's own and is not copied

opinions.topic: new: why God lets babies die
opinions.position: An infant's early death may be God's mercy: foreseeing the evil a life would have held, He withdraws the child before it can be spoiled, like a host leading a guest from a banquet before he drinks himself sick. The innocent infant is not punished.
opinions.side_note: Relevant also to unevangelized: he holds that the unbaptised infant is not tormented but grows toward God.
opinions.today: Deeply divisive and painful: many parents today would find the 'forestalling evil' reason offensive; others find comfort. Use carefully, probably only as reveal material.
opinions.quote: This is that achievement of a perfect Providence which I spoke of; namely, not only to heal evils that have been committed, but also to forestall them before they have been committed; and this, we suspect, is the cause of the deaths of new-born infants.

opinions.position: Doubts should be said aloud and argued out with reasons; he confessed that Scripture's bare command about the soul did not satisfy his mind, and the whole dialogue is built by making him argue the sceptic's side.
opinions.side_note: Pro-questioning. Opposite pole: Ephrem's 'search not out the Lord of the sea'.
opinions.today: Split: many believers today welcome doubt as part of faith; others see it as a danger. Good discriminator.
opinions.quote: In fact, I said that the Divine utterances seemed to me like mere commands compelling us to believe that the soul lasts for ever; not, however, that we were led by them to this belief by any reasoning.
opinions.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection

opinions.topic: new: every person is born royal and free
opinions.position: Human nature was made for rule, not servitude: the soul owns no lord and governs itself by its own will, because it is the image of the God who rules all.
opinions.side_note: Grounds his anti-slavery view and his strong view of free will.
opinions.today: Most modern people accept human dignity and self-rule; some Reformed Christians would stress bondage of the will. Mildly discriminating on free will.
opinions.quote: for the soul immediately shows its royal and exalted character, far removed as it is from the lowliness of private station, in that it owns no lord, and is self-governed, swayed autocratically by its own will; for to whom else does this belong than to a king?

opinions.position: He taught rhetoric for a living as a young man, and Gregory of Nazianzus shamed him for it. Afterwards he used Greek philosophy freely; in the Life of Moses (II.115) he says the 'Egyptian wealth' of pagan learning may be taken and put to God's use.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning (Clement's side). The Life of Moses has no public-domain English; the Nazianzen rebuke is the documented clash.
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept secular learning; some separatist groups do not. One-sided today.
opinions.work: Life of Moses II.115 (secondary); Gregory of Nazianzus, letter to Gregory of Nyssa (Ep. 11)

opinions.position: He preached that the destitute and even lepers must be embraced and cared for as bearers of God's image (On the Love of the Poor, two sermons) and preached against lending at interest (Against the Usurers).
opinions.side_note: Generous side, with Basil and Chrysostom. No public-domain English found for these sermons in this pass.
opinions.today: Everyone approves charity in principle; a statement on usury or on touching lepers discriminates more.
opinions.work: De pauperibus amandis I-II (GNO 9.1); Contra usurarios

sparring.over: Gregory's forged reconciliation letters and his naivety in church politics

Gregory abandoning the Church's service to be a professor of rhetoric: 'preferred to be called a Professor of Rhetoric rather than of Christianity? I, thank God, would rather be the latter than the former.'
sparring.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, letter 'To S. Gregory of Nyssa' (Ep. 11), NPNF2 vol. 7

sparring.over: Whether the Son is of a different, created nature; Gregory wrote twelve books of fierce polemic, Against Eunomius
Precedence and insult: Helladius snubbed him at a martyrs' festival; Gregory appealed to Flavian of Antioch

sparring.with: A rival party in the Jerusalem church
sparring.over: They set up 'another altar' against him after his visit; he defends his orthodoxy against rumours
sparring.source: Letter 17, To Eustathia, Ambrosia and Basilissa

sparring.over: Whether Christ had a human mind; Gregory wrote the Antirrheticus against him (no public-domain English found)

portraits.title: Gregory of Nyssa, Menologion of Basil II
portraits.artist: Byzantine illuminators of the Menologion of Basil II (Vatican Library)

portraits.title: Gregory of Nyssa, Anapafsas monastery, Meteora
portraits.date: Commons says 14th century and 'Theophan the Greek'; the Anapafsas frescoes are usually credited to Theophanes the Cretan (1527). Check before crediting.

figures.name: Ephrem the Syrian
figures.places: Nisibis (Nusaybin, south-east Turkey) until 363, when the city was handed to Persia; then Edessa (Urfa)
figures.role: Deacon (never priest or bishop), teacher, and the great hymn-writer of the Syriac Church; wrote hundreds of hymns (madrashe) and verse homilies, prose refutations of Bardaisan, Mani and Marcion, and a commentary on the Diatessaron
figures.status_note: Saint in every ancient church: Syriac Orthodox, Church of the East, Eastern Orthodox, Catholic (declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XV in 1920), and in the Anglican calendar. Cautions: his hymns contain harsh anti-Jewish polemic; a large body of Greek, Latin and later Syriac writing circulates under his name but is not his ('Ephraem Graecus'); the Syriac Life is late and legendary. Of the NPNF texts, the Nisibene Hymns, the Nativity hymns, The Pearl and the Homily on Our Lord are genuine; the Epiphany hymns and the Homily on Admonition and Repentance are doubted.
figures.hook: When famine hit Edessa, the hermit-deacon came out of his cell, shamed the rich into trusting him with their money, set up some 300 beds in the city's porches, nursed the starving for a year, then went home and died.

stories.story: During a famine at Edessa he asked the rich why they let their wealth rot while people died. They said there was no one honest enough to hand it out. 'What do you think of me?' he asked. They trusted him; he made up about 300 beds in the porticoes, nursed the sick, buried the dead, and went back to his cell when the famine lifted, dying about a month later.
stories.source: Palladius, Lausiac History ch. 40 (trans. W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1918); also Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History 3.16

stories.story: When a town chose him as its bishop and men came to carry him off to be ordained, he ran into the market-place and played the madman, dragging his clothes and eating in public, until they left; he hid until someone else was made bishop.
stories.source: Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History 3.16 (c. 440; 'It is also said')

stories.story: After days of fasting, his attendant dropped his dinner and the dish smashed. Seeing the man terrified, Ephrem said 'Take courage; we will go to the food as the food does not come to us', sat down among the pieces and ate.

The Syrians loved the catchy songs of Harmonius, son of the heretic Bardaisan. Ephrem learned their metres and wrote orthodox hymns to the same tunes, and from then on the Syrians sang his instead. A later Syriac poet, Jacob of Serugh, says he trained choirs of women to sing them.
stories.source: Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History 3.16; Jacob of Serugh, Memra on Ephrem (secondary for the women's choirs)

stories.story: A woman stared at him in the street; he told her to look at the ground. She answered that she was made from man and should look at him, while he, made from earth, should look at the ground. Ephrem was so struck that he wrote the exchange into a book.

He lived through the Persian sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350), when the Persian king dammed the river and flooded the walls, and wrote the Nisibene Hymns as the city's voice pleading with God. In 363 he saw the pagan emperor Julian's body carried past after his defeat, and the city handed to Persia; he left for Edessa.
stories.source: Nisibene Hymns 1-3 (NPNF2 vol. 13); Hymns against Julian 3 (secondary; no public-domain English)

temperament.trait: Hot-tempered by nature, gentle by choice
temperament.evidence: 'although he was naturally prone to passion, he never exhibited angry feeling toward any one from the period of his embracing a monastic life.'

temperament.trait: Loved quiet; wary to the point of severity
temperament.evidence: 'He was particularly fond of tranquillity. He was so serious and so careful to avoid giving occasion to calumny, that he refrained from the very sight of women.'
Sozomen says he 'was totally exempt from the love of vainglory' and faked madness to escape being made a bishop; he stayed a deacon.

'For I did not wish that a letter should pass between us, since it cannot ask or be asked questions ; but I had wished that there might pass between us a discourse from mouth to ear, asking and being asked questions.'
temperament.source: First Discourse to Hypatius, in Prose Refutations of Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan, trans. C. W. Mitchell (1912)

temperament.trait: Dramatic and playful even about death
temperament.evidence: In the Nisibene Hymns Death and Satan bicker and complain like two losers; Death moans that Jesus has put him on a diet.

genuine_lines.quote: Search out the sea, but search not out the Lord of the sea!
genuine_lines.translation: J. B. Morris, rev. A. E. Johnston, NPNF2 vol. 13 (1898)

genuine_lines.quote: Gluttonous Death, lamented and said, I have learned fasting, which I used not to know
genuine_lines.location: Hymn 35 (as divided on New Advent), stanza 6
genuine_lines.translation: J. T. Sarsfield Stopford, NPNF2 vol. 13 (1898)

genuine_lines.quote: The prayer of your inhabitants, sufficed for your deliverance; it was not that they were righteous, but that they were penitent
Why do you not take pity on human nature being destroyed, instead of letting your wealth be corrupted for the condemnation of your souls?
humble utterances overcame him, whom mighty wonders had not overcome.

misattributed.line: The Prayer of St Ephrem: 'O Lord and Master of my life, take from me the spirit of sloth, despair, lust of power, and idle talk...'
misattributed.truth: Beloved and prayed daily in Orthodox Lent, but it comes from the Greek Ephrem corpus ('Ephraem Graecus'), written in Greek long after him; no Syriac original is known.

misattributed.line: 'All the saints and elect of God are gathered before the tribulation ... and are taken to the Lord' (quoted as early proof of a pre-tribulation rapture).
misattributed.truth: From a Latin sermon 'On the Last Times' by 'Pseudo-Ephraem', probably 6th-7th century, not by Ephrem.

misattributed.line: Stories that he visited Basil in Caesarea and the monks of Egypt.
misattributed.truth: From the late, legendary Syriac Life. Sozomen says only that Basil admired him.

misattributed.line: Lines quoted from the Homily on Admonition and Repentance and the Hymns for the Epiphany in NPNF vol. 13.
misattributed.truth: Printed under his name, but their authenticity is doubted by modern editors. Use the Nisibene Hymns, the Nativity hymns, The Pearl and the Homily on Our Lord for anything load-bearing.

opinions.position: Do not pry into God. Study creation all you like, but prying into the Godhead with 'all manner of questions' blinds faith; the diver does not dissect his pearl. Disputation and prayer cannot share one mouth.
opinions.side_note: Against probing: mystery is received with praise, not dissected. Aimed at the Arian 'searchers'. Opposite pole to Gregory of Nyssa's argued doubts.
opinions.today: Split: many believers today encourage hard questions; others value mystery and simple trust. Strong discriminator.
opinions.quote: Search out the sea, but search not out the Lord of the sea!

opinions.position: Hoarded wealth during a famine is the rich man's condemnation; a hermit should leave his cell to make the rich give, and to run the relief himself.
opinions.side_note: Generous and hands-on. Contrast Isaac the Syrian, who told solitaries not to go collecting for the poor.
opinions.today: Everyone approves helping in a famine; the discriminating part is 'a contemplative should drop prayer for practical relief' versus 'keep to your calling'.
opinions.quote: Why do you not take pity on human nature being destroyed, instead of letting your wealth be corrupted for the condemnation of your souls?

opinions.position: Flee high office: he refused to be made bishop, faking madness to escape, and stayed a deacon all his life.
opinions.side_note: Avoid office. Reported conduct (Sozomen, c. 440, 'It is also said'), not his own words.
opinions.today: People split between 'step up and lead' and 'distrust anyone who wants power'. Discriminating.
opinions.quote: He was appointed bishop of some town, and attempts were made to convey him away for the purpose of ordaining him. As soon as he became aware of what was intended, he ran to the market-place, and showed himself as a madman

opinions.position: Use the popular music of the day, even the heretics' own catchy tunes, and fill it with true teaching; the Church should out-sing its rivals.
opinions.side_note: Pro popular music in worship. Opposite pole to those who wanted only psalms or plain chant (and to Augustine's worry about enjoying the tune).
opinions.today: Split: contemporary worship versus traditional hymns and chant is a live argument in churches today. Strong discriminator.
opinions.quote: When Ephraim perceived that the Syrians were charmed with the elegance of the diction and the rhythm of the melody, he became apprehensive, lest they should imbibe the same opinions; and therefore, although he was ignorant of Grecian learning, he applied himself to the understanding of the metres of Harmonius, and composed similar poems in accordance with the doctrines of the Church

opinions.position: A hot temper can be tamed; he met a servant's clumsy accident with kindness and a joke instead of a rebuke.
opinions.side_note: Against anger. Reported by Sozomen.
opinions.today: One-sided (everyone admires this); useful as reveal material.
opinions.quote: Take courage; we will go to the food as the food does not come to us

opinions.position: In a siege, the city is saved by repentance and prayer, not by its own righteousness; war is God's rod on a sinful people, and sackcloth wins crowns.
opinions.side_note: Not a pacifism statement: he reads war as providence and chastisement, and prayer as the true defence. He also celebrated the fall of the pagan Julian (secondary).
opinions.today: Few today would read a war as God's punishment of a city; many believers still say prayer matters in war. Discriminating on 'disasters as judgement'.
opinions.quote: The prayer of your inhabitants, sufficed for your deliverance; it was not that they were righteous, but that they were penitent

opinions.position: Floods, sieges and breaches in the wall are God's chastening, meant to teach and to bring a people to repentance; He struck the stones to spare the bodies.
opinions.side_note: Yes side.
opinions.today: Sharply divided: many Christians and most secular people reject reading disasters as judgement; some believers still do. Strong discriminator.
opinions.quote: For instead of souls that feel, He smote the stones that feel not, that He might chasten us. In His love He spared our bodies, and hasted to smite our wall.

opinions.position: A notorious sinner's few tears outweigh a respectable man's small love; the penitent woman was forgiven while her host was rebuked.
opinions.side_note: Yes to second chances, generously.
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle; discriminates only when the sinner is notorious.
opinions.quote: Thus he that had invited Him to the great banquet was rebuked because of the smallness of his love; but she by her few tears atoned for the many follies of her offenses.
opinions.location: the sinful woman at Simon's house

opinions.position: Correct people as a friend, gently and humbly; Christ won the proud Pharisee with a humble word where miracles had failed.
opinions.side_note: Gentle correction side.
opinions.today: Most agree gentleness works better; discriminates against 'call it out bluntly' temperaments.
opinions.quote: Love and reproof can be discerned here. For this is a word of love such as friends use with their friends.
opinions.location: on 'Simon, I have somewhat to say unto you'

opinions.topic: new: free will against fate and the stars
opinions.position: Human beings are free; speech itself was given free so that it could serve our free will. He fought Bardaisan's teaching that fate and the stars govern much of life.
opinions.side_note: Strong free-will side against astrological fate.
opinions.today: Many people today, including some Christians, read horoscopes or feel life is fated; most Christians affirm free will. Discriminating, and 'do the stars shape us?' is a question people enjoy.
opinions.quote: For the Deity gave us Speech that is free like Itself, in order that free Speech might serve our independent Freewill.
opinions.translation: C. W. Mitchell, S. Ephraim's Prose Refutations of Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan, vol. 1 (1912)

opinions.position: Death is a beaten thief: since Christ, Death laments while the dead are made to rejoice, so Christian grief is shot through with triumph.
opinions.side_note: Hope side; expressed through mockery of Death.
opinions.today: Believers mostly agree; secular people do not. Discriminates on belief rather than temperament.
opinions.quote: Gluttonous Death, lamented and said, I have learned fasting, which I used not to know

opinions.position: Rein in laughter and merriment; be sad only for your sins, and let sorrow and hope govern mirth.
opinions.side_note: Sober side. CAUTION: from the Homily on Admonition and Repentance, whose authenticity is doubted.
opinions.today: Most people today value laughter highly; a 'restrain laughter' statement would split sharply. Use only if another genuine source is found.
opinions.quote: Restrain laughter by suffering, and mirthfulness by sorrow. Console suffering by hope, and sadness by expectation.

opinions.position: He trained choirs of women to sing his doctrinal hymns in church.
opinions.side_note: Pro women singing and teaching through song. Source is Jacob of Serugh's verse homily on Ephrem (c. 500), not Ephrem himself.
opinions.today: Uncontroversial in most churches; still debated in some traditions. Better as reveal colour.
opinions.work: Jacob of Serugh, Memra on Mar Ephrem

opinions.position: Each word of Scripture holds more meanings than any reader can drain, like a spring a thirsty man drinks from without exhausting; no one should think his reading is the only one.
opinions.side_note: Many senses side. Commentary on the Diatessaron 1.18-19 (English only in McCarthy, 1993, copyrighted).
opinions.today: Split between 'one plain meaning' and 'many layers'. Discriminating.

opinions.position: Nature and Scripture are two witnesses to God; creation is a second book to read.
opinions.side_note: Hymns on Paradise 5 and Hymns on Virginity 20 (English only in Brock and McVey, copyrighted). The same idea appears in the doubtful Homily on Admonition: 'Let nature be your book, and all creation your tables'.
opinions.today: Widely shared; one-sided.
opinions.work: Hymns on Paradise 5; Hymns on Virginity 20

opinions.position: He wrote hymns rejoicing at the death of the pagan emperor Julian and welcoming the Christian emperor Jovian, reading the empire's fortunes as a judgement on idolatry.
opinions.side_note: Pro Christian empire. Hymns against Julian (McVey 1989, copyrighted).
opinions.today: Split between those who want a Christian public order and those who want church and state apart.

sparring.over: Fate, the stars and the soul; Ephrem wrote rival hymns to their tunes and prose refutations

sparring.with: Mani and Marcion (their followers in Edessa)
sparring.over: Whether the body and the material world are evil, and whether the Creator is a lesser god
sparring.source: Discourses to Hypatius and Against Marcion (Mitchell 1912-1921)

sparring.over: Prying into the Son's generation; the Hymns on Faith attack their method as much as their doctrine

figures.name: Isaac the Syrian
figures.places: Born in Beth Qatraye (the Qatar region of the Gulf); bishop of Nineveh (Mosul); then the mountains of Beth Huzaye (Khuzistan, south-west Iran) and the monastery of Rabban Shabur
figures.role: Monk, briefly bishop, then hermit and writer of ascetical and mystical homilies in Syriac
figures.status_note: A bishop of the Church of the East (historically called 'Nestorian' by its rivals). His writings were translated into Greek at Mar Saba in the 8th-9th century and became treasured in Eastern Orthodox monasticism; he is commemorated on 28 January in the Orthodox calendar and read across the Syriac churches. He is not on the Roman calendar. Cautions: he calls Theodore of Mopsuestia 'the light of the whole world' and quotes 'the blessed Euagrius', both condemned in 553; the Greek translators blurred this. His Second Part (rediscovered 1983) openly hopes that Gehenna will end for all. A later bishop, Daniel bar Tubanitha, opposed his teaching.
figures.hook: Made bishop of Nineveh, he quit after five months and spent the rest of his life in the mountains, writing that a merciful heart burns with love for every creature, animals, enemies and even demons, until it cannot bear to hear of anything suffering.

stories.story: Consecrated bishop of Nineveh by the Catholicos George, he abdicated after five months, the earliest source says for reasons known to God, and retired to the monastery of Rabban Shabur, where he died old and blind 'through study and austerity'.
stories.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'Isaac of Nineveh', summarising Isho'dnah of Basra's Book of Chastity (9th century)

stories.story: A later tradition explains the resignation: two men came to him over a debt; the creditor, told of the Gospel's command to lend without demanding back, said 'leave the Gospel out of it', and Isaac answered that if the Gospel was to be left aside there was nothing for him to do there, and left. This is hagiographical tradition, not the earliest source.

Arguing that even hermits must care for the sick near them, he retells how Macarius the Great, at ninety, walked forty miles from Scetis to Alexandria to swap his dry bread for the fresh loaf a sick monk wanted, and how Agathon nursed a sick stranger in a rented house for six months.
stories.source: Mystic Treatises, 'An answer to a brother ... that it is not becoming to neglect the distressed and sick when they are near' (Wensinck 1923)

temperament.evidence: 'Be not angry with me for telling thee the truth: thou never hast sought this within thy soul.'
temperament.source: Mystic Treatises, 'Short sentences concerning the distinction ...'

temperament.trait: Humble about originality, a lifelong learner
temperament.evidence: 'For we have not forgotten that we are not above the rank of disciples so long as we dwell in the flesh.'
temperament.source: Mystic Treatises XXVI, 'Against those who say: If God is good wherefore has He made these things?'

temperament.trait: Speaks from experience and expects to be doubted
temperament.evidence: 'I shall tell thee a thing at which thou must not laugh; for I tell the truth.'

temperament.trait: A reader to the point of blindness; withdrew from power
temperament.evidence: He resigned his see after five months and died 'blind through study and austerity'.

misattributed.line: Acquire the Spirit of peace, and thousands around you will be saved.
misattributed.truth: St Seraphim of Sarov (19th-century Russia), sometimes posted under Isaac's name. Isaac's related line is 'be at peace with thy soul; then heaven and earth will be at peace with thee'.

misattributed.line: Popular Isaac quotations in the wording 'Be at peace with your own soul...', 'This life has been given to you for repentance...', 'The one who has been made worthy to see himself...'
misattributed.truth: These are the wording of the Holy Transfiguration Monastery translation (1984, copyrighted). Some are genuine in substance; quote Wensinck's 1923 wording or check the Syriac.

misattributed.line: The creditor story ('leave the Gospel out of it') as the documented reason he resigned.
misattributed.truth: The earliest source, Isho'dnah of Basra, gives no reason. The story is later tradition.

opinions.topic: new: compassion for animals and all creatures
opinions.position: True mercy burns for the whole creation: people, birds, beasts, reptiles, enemies of the truth, even demons. The merciful person cannot bear to hear of the smallest suffering of any creature and prays for all of them with tears.
opinions.side_note: Wide mercy side. Almost unique among the Fathers in naming animals, reptiles and demons.
opinions.today: Most people today warm to kindness to animals; 'even the demons' and 'enemies of the truth' will split believers. Good discriminator if phrased about enemies and animals.
opinions.quote: And what is a merciful heart? He replied: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists

opinions.position: Hell is not God withholding love: the damned are tormented by love itself, by knowing they sinned against love. In his First Part he says hell's end 'is not known'; in his Second Part (Syriac, found 1983) he openly hopes Gehenna will end and all be restored.
opinions.side_note: Hopeful/universalist side, strongest in Part II (secondary here: only Brock's modern English exists).
opinions.today: Split, as for Gregory of Nyssa; 'hell is love experienced as torment' appeals to many Orthodox readers today.
opinions.quote: Also I say that even those who are scourged in Hell are tormented with the scourgings of love. Scourgings for love's sake, namely of those who perceive that they have sinned against love, are more hard and bitter than tortures through fear.
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.topic: new: will sin and hell ever end?
opinions.position: Sin, hell and death are not things God made; sin had a beginning and will one day not be; hell began, but its end is not known; death will vanish altogether.
opinions.side_note: Open question in Part I, leaning hopeful.
opinions.today: Divides traditional and hopeful believers.
opinions.quote: Sin is the fruit of will. There was a time, when it was not. And there will be a time, when it will not be. Hell is the fruit of sin ; at some time or other it had beginning; but its end is not known.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises XXVI, 'Against those who say: If God is good wherefore has He made these things?'

opinions.position: Do not scold or direct anyone, even the very wicked. Throw your cloak over the sinner and cover him; if you cannot take his punishment for him, at least take the shame rather than expose him.
opinions.side_note: Strongly against correcting others. Opposite pole to Jerome or Gregory of Nyssa's letter to Flavian.
opinions.today: Split: 'cover a brother's faults' versus 'expose wrongdoing'. A very good discriminator, especially after church abuse scandals, so frame it about everyday faults.
opinions.quote: Do not vituperate any one and do not direct any one, not even those who are very evil in their behaviour. Spread thy mantle over the sinner and cover him.
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.position: Do not hate the sinner at all, not even 'for his sins'; we are all condemned. Weep for him and pray for him, as Christ wept over Jerusalem.
opinions.side_note: Against even the 'hate the sin' framing as a cover for hatred.
opinions.today: Most people say they agree; the sharp edge ('don't even say you hate his sins') splits.
opinions.quote: we are all worthy of condemnation. If thou art moved for the sake of God, weep over him. Why shouldst thou hate him? Thou meanst to hate his sins? Pray on his behalf, that thou mayest resemble Christ, who was not angry with sinners but prayed on their behalf.
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.position: Even zeal for the faith is no licence for anger. If you want to turn someone to the truth, suffer for him and speak with tears and love, with no hostility on your face.
opinions.side_note: Against righteous anger, even for doctrine.
opinions.today: Split: many admire 'righteous anger'; others distrust it. Good discriminator.
opinions.quote: And with tears and in love thou must speak to him without being enraged against him, effacing all sign of hostility from thy face. Love does not know how to be angry ; it is not indignant, it does not despise so as to cause suffering.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.position: Never write anyone off: the sinner you look down on may within a short time outrun you and come nearer to God than you.
opinions.side_note: Yes to second chances.
opinions.today: Widely agreed in principle; useful in combination with a harder statement.
opinions.quote: Why doest thou rebuke the sinner, o man? The labours of thine own merchandise have not yet entered the harbour; the hope of him over whom thou art extolling thyself, has not been cut off by God. It is possible that within a short time he will surpass thee in excellence and come nearer to God than thou art.
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.position: Mercy that stays within justice is not mercy; the merciful person gladly lets himself be wronged rather than insist on his full rights.
opinions.side_note: Mercy over fairness. Clear opposite to anyone who says fairness comes first.
opinions.today: Strongly split today (fairness versus grace); an excellent everyday statement: 'I would rather be cheated than insist on what I am owed.'
opinions.quote: But I say : if the merciful be not even above justice, he is not merciful. This means, that he will not only show mercy unto men on his own part, but that he will volun- tarily suffer iniquity with delight
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan
opinions.translation: A. J. Wensinck (1923); the hyphen in 'volun- tarily' is a line-break in the scan

opinions.position: The passions only quiet down in the desert; withdrawal from the world is the way to God. But the solitude is inward: be friendly to all, alone in your mind.
opinions.side_note: Strongly pro-solitude, with an inward twist.
opinions.today: Most people today prize company and community; a minority crave solitude. Good discriminator ('I need long stretches alone').
opinions.quote: Be a friend of all men, but a solitary in thy mind.
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.topic: new: rules versus a neighbour in need
opinions.position: A hermit far from people need not go out looking for the sick. But one who lives near people and sees a brother in trouble and hides behind his rule of solitude is merciless: a 'sham solitude'.
opinions.side_note: Need beats rule when need is at the door.
opinions.today: Most agree; discriminates when framed as 'I keep my commitments/boundaries even when someone needs me'.
opinions.quote: But if he see the brother according to the flesh and to profession, in trouble, or rather: Christ rejected and vexed, and he flee and hide himself, pretending a sham solitude — he that acts thus, is without mercy.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, 'An answer to a brother ... that it is not becoming to neglect the distressed and sick when they are near'
opinions.location: Bedjan p. 568 (margin number in the scan)

opinions.position: Silence belongs to the world to come; speech belongs to this one. Silence and fasting are the core of a hidden life with God.
opinions.side_note: Strongly pro-silence.
opinions.today: Split: extroverts and introverts divide; many today seek silence retreats. Good discriminator.
opinions.quote: Silence is a symbol of the future world. Speech is an organ of this world.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, 'A letter which he sent to his friend ...'
opinions.location: page not fixed in this pass; search the quoted words in the scan

opinions.position: If you have anything, give it away at once; if you have nothing, do not want it. But one who has renounced the world should not go back into handling money and collecting for the poor: his calling is higher than the almsgiver's.
opinions.side_note: Radical poverty, but contemplation over fundraising. Opposite to Ephrem leaving his cell to run famine relief.
opinions.today: Split: 'prayer is the greater work' versus 'faith must be practical'. Good discriminator.
opinions.quote: Thy rank is higher than that of almsgivers. I pray thee, do not make thyself an object of laughter. The latter is the class of adolescents being educated ; the former is the way of per- fection. If thou possessest, spend at once. If not, be not desirous to possess.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence

opinions.position: Knowledge that comes from practice is trustworthy; clever words without experience are cheap. Wisdom can talk well about virtue without ever having lived it.
opinions.side_note: Experience over book learning (though he read constantly and loved Theodore's commentaries).
opinions.today: Most people agree experience beats theory; mildly discriminating.
opinions.quote: Very different is the word of practice from words of beauty. Even without experience wisdom knows how to adorn its words and to speak the truth even without having any acquaintance with it, and to express itself concerning excellence without any experience of [practical] performance. A word proceeding from practice, is a treasure to confide in.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence

opinions.position: Keep away from books that sharpen the differences between the confessions to cause schism; they arm the spirit of slander against your soul.
opinions.side_note: Against sectarian polemic, from a man whose own church was isolated.
opinions.today: Split: many enjoy apologetics and debate; others avoid it. Good discriminator ('I enjoy a good argument about doctrine').
opinions.quote: Let thy arms be: fasting and tears which thou shedst in constant self-humiliation-, and prudence against reading books which accentuate the differences between the confessions, with the aim of causing schisms, which provides the spirit of slander with a mighty weapon against the soul.
opinions.work: Mystic Treatises, Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence

opinions.position: No prayer is answered faster than the prayer to be reconciled with someone angry at you, especially when you take the blame yourself.
opinions.side_note: Take the blame to make peace.
opinions.today: Split between 'take the blame to keep the peace' and 'don't apologise for what isn't your fault'. Good discriminator.
opinions.quote: There is no prayer which is heard so soon as when a man asks to be reconciled with those who are angry with him. And when a man charges himself with the fault, this prayer is answered without delay.
